name: Robert Crawford
credit: No confirmed portrait sourced for this archive.
bio: Robert Crawford was a Scottish songwriter who contributed to Allan Ramsay's Tea-Table Miscellany. Gilfillan records that he was drowned while returning from France in 1733.
His song The Bush aboon Traquair is one of the early Scots songs of the eighteenth century revival.

poems.title: The Bush Aboon Traquair
poems.author: Robert Crawford
poems.collection: Specimens with Memoirs of the Less-known British Poets, ed. George Gilfillan (1860)
poems.text:
Hear me, ye nymphs, and every swain,
I'll tell how Peggy grieves me;
Though thus I languish and complain,
Alas! she ne'er believes me.
My vows and sighs, like silent air,
Unheeded, never move her;
At the bonnie Bush aboon Traquair,
'Twas there I first did love her.

That day she smiled and made me glad,
No maid seemed ever kinder;
I thought myself the luckiest lad,
So sweetly there to find her;
I tried to soothe my amorous flame,
In words that I thought tender;
If more there passed, I'm not to blame--
I meant not to offend her.

Yet now she scornful flies the plain,
The fields we then frequented;
If e'er we meet she shows disdain,
She looks as ne'er acquainted.
The bonnie bush bloomed fair in May,
Its sweets I'll aye remember;
But now her frowns make it decay--
It fades as in December.

Ye rural powers, who hear my strains,
Why thus should Peggy grieve me?
Oh, make her partner in my pains,
Then let her smiles relieve me!
If not, my love will turn despair,
My passion no more tender;
I'll leave the Bush aboon Traquair--
To lonely wilds I'll wander.
